questions.q: In the lesson's web app, what happens when the form is posted to the /predict route?
options: The model is retrained on the submitted values
The form values are gathered, converted to a numpy array and sent to the model, which returns a prediction
The values are stored in a spreadsheet for a data scientist to review
The page reloads without contacting the model
questions.explain: The Flask route turns form input into the array shape the model expects and returns its prediction.
questions.evidence: The form variables are gathered and converted to a numpy array.

questions.q: What is the generative AI application lifecycle?
options: A licence for using large language models
A list of approved AI vendors
A framework that guides you through developing, deploying and maintaining a generative AI application
questions.explain: It structures goals, measurement, challenges and solutions across the life of an AI application.
questions.evidence: The generative AI lifecycle is a framework that guides you through the stages of developing, deploying, and maintaining a generative AI application.

questions.q: What does static (offline) training mean?
options: You train the model continuously or at least frequently
You train the model only once
You train a separate model for each user
You train the model on the production server
questions.explain: Static training is simpler but the model can go stale; dynamic training keeps learning from fresh data.
questions.evidence: Static training (also called offline training ) means that you train a model only once.

questions.q: What does dynamic (online) inference mean?
options: The model only makes predictions on demand, for example when a client requests one
All predictions are computed in advance and cached
The model is retrained before every prediction
Predictions are made by people, not the model
questions.explain: Dynamic inference handles diverse, real-time requests; static inference precomputes and caches predictions.
questions.evidence: Dynamic inference (also called online inference or real-time inference) means that the model only makes predictions on demand, for example, when a client requests a prediction.

questions.q: How can you make sure a model is compatible with its serving infrastructure before release?
options: Deploy it straight to production and watch the logs
Stage the model in a sandboxed server environment to avoid dependency conflicts
Convert it to a spreadsheet formula
questions.explain: A sandboxed staging environment surfaces dependency conflicts without affecting users.
questions.evidence: Ensure model-infrastructure compatibility by staging the model in a sandboxed server environment to avoid dependency conflicts.

questions.q: How should a production ML pipeline monitor its raw input data?
options: Only check the data once, when the model is first trained
Trust the data if the model's accuracy is high
Ask users to report bad data
Continuously check it against expected values by writing rules the data must satisfy
questions.explain: A data schema with rules (for example ratings must be 1–5) catches broken inputs early.
questions.evidence: To monitor your data, you should continuously check it against expected statistical values by writing rules that the data must satisfy.

questions.q: In MLOps model validation, when is a model considered adequate for deployment?
options: When its predictive performance is better than a certain baseline
When it is larger than the previous model
When a data scientist has run it in a notebook
questions.explain: Validation compares the candidate model against a baseline before it can replace the current one.
questions.evidence: Model validation: The model is confirmed to be adequate for deployment—that its predictive performance is better than a certain baseline.

questions.q: What are 'data values skews', and what do they call for?
options: Significant changes in the statistical properties of data — a trigger to retrain the model
Typos in column names — a trigger to rename features
Slow queries — a trigger to add servers
Missing labels — a trigger to delete the data
questions.explain: When data patterns change, the model must be retrained to capture them.
questions.evidence: Data values skews: These skews are significant changes in the statistical properties of data, which means that data patterns are changing, and you need to trigger a retraining of the model to capture these changes.

questions.q: According to the Rules of Machine Learning, what must you trust before doing imaginative machine learning?
questions.explain: Start with simple, testable infrastructure; otherwise it is hard to tell what is going wrong.
questions.evidence: it will be hard to figure out what is happening if you don’t first trust your pipeline.

questions.q: What is the best way to deal with training-serving skew?
options: Explicitly monitor it so system and data changes don't introduce skew unnoticed
questions.explain: Skew between training and serving data creeps in silently unless you measure it.
questions.evidence: The best solution is to explicitly monitor it so that system and data changes don’t introduce skew unnoticed.

questions.q: Besides goals and performance, what does the generative AI lifecycle help you align your application with?
options: The ethical and legal standards of your domain and stakeholders
The colour scheme of your website
questions.explain: Following the lifecycle keeps the app delivering value responsibly.
questions.evidence: It also helps you to align your application with the ethical and legal standards of your domain and your stakeholders.

questions.q: Compared with classic MLOps, whom does LLMOps focus on?
options: App developers who integrate models offered as a service
questions.explain: Integration with Models-as-a-Service is a key point.
questions.evidence: in LLMOps, we are more focused on the App Developers, using integrations as a key point

questions.q: Why must feature-engineered data be checked separately from raw input data?
options: It can be very different from the raw data
questions.explain: Problems can appear during feature engineering itself.
questions.evidence: Because feature engineered data can be very different from raw input data, you must check feature engineered data separately from your checks on raw input data.

questions.q: What are data slices?
options: Subsets of the data, such as one region, whose performance you track separately
questions.explain: Good average performance can hide poor performance on a slice.
questions.evidence: are called data slices

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a data validation rule?
options: User-submitted ratings are always between 1 and 5
The model must be trained on a GPU
questions.explain: Rules check data against expected values continuously.
questions.evidence: Ensure that user-submitted ratings are always in the range 1 to 5.

questions.q: How does continuous integration (CI) differ for ML systems?
options: It is not used in ML
It only runs once a year
It also tests and validates data, schemas and models, not just code
questions.explain: ML systems can break when the data changes, even if the code doesn't.
questions.evidence: CI is no longer only about testing and validating code and components, but also testing and validating data, data schemas, and models.

questions.q: How does continuous delivery (CD) differ for ML systems?
options: It only copies a single file
It is done by hand each time
It deploys a training pipeline that automatically deploys a prediction service
It deploys the dataset to users
questions.explain: The pipeline itself becomes the product being delivered.
questions.evidence: CD is no longer about a single software package or a service, but a system (an ML training pipeline) that should automatically deploy another service (model prediction service).

questions.q: What does continuous training (CT) mean at MLOps level 1?
options: Data scientists retrain it by hand every year
The model is retrained automatically in production on fresh data, triggered by the pipeline
questions.explain: Triggers can be schedules, new data or performance drops.
questions.evidence: The model is automatically trained in production using fresh data based on live pipeline triggers

questions.q: What is experimental-operational symmetry?
options: Using the same pipeline in development, preproduction and production
Running two models side by side
questions.explain: It is key to unifying MLOps with DevOps.
questions.evidence: The pipeline implementation that is used in the development or experiment environment is used in the preproduction and production environment

questions.q: What does a feature store help data scientists do?
options: Discover and reuse feature sets instead of re-creating them
questions.explain: It also keeps features consistent between training and serving.
questions.evidence: Discover and reuse available feature sets for their entities, instead of re-creating the same or similar ones.

questions.q: At MLOps level 2, how is the pipeline executed in production?
options: Only when a manager approves by email
Automatically, on a schedule or in response to a trigger
questions.explain: Full CI/CD automation lets teams update pipelines rapidly.
questions.evidence: The pipeline is automatically executed in production based on a schedule or in response to a trigger.

questions.q: Where is the trained model pushed after automated training?
questions.explain: The registry tracks model versions ready for deployment.
questions.evidence: The output of this stage is a trained model that is pushed to the model registry.

questions.q: Why encapsulate the learning parts of an ML system?
options: So you can test everything around them
To hide the model from users
questions.explain: Testable infrastructure builds trust in the pipeline.
questions.evidence: Make sure that the infrastructure is testable, and that the learning parts of the system are encapsulated so that you can test everything around it.

questions.q: A pipeline drops older posts. Why can that data be useless for some models?
options: The negative examples are gone, so you can't model why posts weren't seen
questions.explain: Understand what your pipeline filters out.
questions.evidence: this data is useless if we want to model why a particular post was not seen by the user, because all the negative examples have been dropped

questions.q: In the first phase of an ML system's life, what are the important issues?
options: Getting training data in, instrumenting metrics and building serving infrastructure
questions.explain: Fancy modelling comes later.
questions.evidence: In the first phase of the lifecycle of a machine learning system, the important issues are to get the training data into the learning system, get any metrics of interest instrumented, and create a serving infrastructure.

questions.q: Should you expect your current model to be the last one you launch?
options: No — expect to keep launching, and avoid complexity that slows future launches
questions.explain: New features, regularisation and objectives all lead to new launches.
questions.evidence: expect that the model you are working on now will be the last one that you will launch

questions.q: What is 'fishfooding'?
options: Using a prototype within your own team
Using a prototype across the whole company
Releasing a model to all users
questions.explain: Dogfooding means using it within your company.
questions.evidence: fishfooding (using a prototype within your team) and dogfooding (using a prototype within your company)

questions.q: Why might an all-male team design a 35-year-old female user persona?
options: Because personas are required by law
To train the model on one user
To look at results from a perspective unlike the team's own
questions.explain: Your team is not a representative sample of users.
questions.evidence: if your team is all male, it might help to design a 35-year-old female user persona

questions.q: What does Alice realise about launch decisions?
options: They are made by the model itself
They depend on many criteria, only some of which ML can optimise directly
questions.explain: There are no 'hit points' showing a product's health.
questions.evidence: launch decisions depend on multiple criteria, only some of which can be directly optimized using ML

questions.q: If product goals aren't covered by the existing algorithmic objective, what should you do?
options: Change either the objective or the product goals
questions.explain: Objective and goals must line up.
questions.evidence: if the product goals are not covered by the existing algorithmic objective, you need to change either your objective or your product goals

questions.q: What is a container image?
options: The template from which container instances are created
A running copy of a container
questions.explain: One image can start many containers.
questions.evidence: a container image is the template from which particular instances of containers will be created

questions.q: After the hello-world container finishes running, what remains?
options: The container image, with nothing actively running
questions.explain: Containers are transient; images are long-lived.
questions.evidence: The container image is still there, but nothing is actively running.

questions.q: What does the hello container do by default?
options: Runs a default action: printing a message
questions.explain: Images can define a default command to run.
questions.evidence: The hello container is set up to run an action by default

questions.q: What is a Dockerfile?
options: A plain text file of keywords and commands used to build a container image
questions.explain: It is a reproducible recipe for an image.
questions.evidence: A Dockerfile is a plain text file with keywords and commands that can be used to create a new container image.

questions.q: Are changes made inside an interactive container saved to a new image by default?
questions.explain: Exiting the container discards them unless you snapshot it.
questions.evidence: Once we exit, these changes are not saved to a new container image by default.

questions.q: Why is snapshotting an interactive container a poor way to build images?
questions.explain: A Dockerfile records every step so anyone can rebuild the image.
questions.evidence: building container images this way is not easily reproducible

questions.q: How do a Dockerfile and a Containerfile differ?
options: Only in the file name — Podman can use both
questions.explain: The keywords and commands are the same.
questions.evidence: The two are essentially identical, differing only in the file name used, and Podman is capable of using both.
